name: Retro Game Launcher
description: A web application to browse, manage, and launch your retro game collection. It allows configuring platforms, emulators, and game details. (ROM scanning and launching are simulated).

games.title: Jet Set Willy II : The Final Frontier
games.description: This platform game is the sequel of Jet Set Willy. Again has each room its own hazards, such as spikes, revolving razors and ropes. The route through the house must be navigated carefully, due to the multiple entrances to some rooms - this is perhaps the first action game where mapping is an advantage. Another innovation, to the chagrin of players everywhere, is manual protection - a sheet of colour-coded numbers.

games.title: Manic Miner
games.description: You play the role of Miner Willy, a bold explorer and adventurer. He discovers a network of underground caverns used by an advanced but now extinct civilization, and realizes that the mines contain lucrative metal ores. Through 20 caverns, you must collect all treasures before all time (air) runs out, watching out for the nasty guardians, the obstacles, dead falls, quicksands and all elements to be found in a classic platform game.

platforms.name: Acorn ATOM
platforms.description: The Acorn ATOM was a British home computer released in 1980. It was designed by Acorn Computers Ltd, the same company behind the BBC Micro. The ATOM was aimed at the hobbyist and educational market, offering a more affordable alternative to some of its competitors. It featured a Motorola 6502 processor, a relatively high resolution display for its time, and a BASIC interpreter built into its ROM. Users could expand its capabilities through various interfaces and expansion cards, including cassette tape for storage and an optional disk drive. While not as widely popular as the BBC Micro or Commodore's offerings, the ATOM played a role in the early home computer revolution in the UK and helped establish Acorn's presence in the market.

platforms.name: Sinclair ZX-Spectrum
platforms.description: The Sinclair ZX Spectrum, often simply called the Spectrum, was an 8-bit personal home computer launched in the United Kingdom in 1982 by Sinclair Research. It was known for its iconic rubber keyboard, distinctive rainbow stripes, and relatively low price, making it accessible to a wide audience. The Spectrum played a significant role in popularizing home computing and video gaming in the UK and Europe, with a vast library of games that pushed the limits of its hardware, including titles like 'Jet Set Willy', 'Manic Miner', and 'Elite'. The Spectrum's simple design and affordable cost fueled a flourishing homebrew software scene, with many programmers creating games and utilities in BASIC and machine code.

platforms.name: Dragon 32/64
platforms.description: The Dragon 32 and Dragon 64 were home computers produced in the early 1980s, primarily for the UK and Australian markets. They were designed as clones of the Tandy TRS-80 Color Computer, sharing a similar architecture and functionality. The main difference between the two models was the amount of RAM, with the Dragon 32 having 32KB and the Dragon 64 boasting 64KB. Both machines featured a Motorola 6809E processor, a custom sound chip, and a built-in BASIC programming language. They were popular for educational purposes and for playing a wide range of games, and had good graphics for the time. Although not as successful as some competitors, the Dragon computers provided a capable and affordable entry point into home computing.

platforms.name: Sony Playstation 3
platforms.description: The PlayStation 3 (PS3) is a home video game console developed by Sony Computer Entertainment. Released in 2006, it competed with Microsoft's Xbox 360 and Nintendo's Wii during the seventh generation of video game consoles. The PS3 boasted a powerful Cell processor and a Blu-ray Disc drive, allowing it to play high-definition movies and games. It offered online gaming services through PlayStation Network, providing access to downloadable games, demos, and online multiplayer experiences. The console went through several hardware revisions, including the "Slim" and "Super Slim" models, refining its design and adding features over its lifespan. It played a significant role in the gaming industry and helped popularize Blu-ray technology.

platforms.name: Atari Jaguar
platforms.description: The Atari Jaguar is a home video game console released by Atari Corporation in 1993. It was marketed as the first 64-bit system, though its architecture was more complex and arguably less powerful than some of its contemporaries. Despite ambitious marketing, the Jaguar faced several challenges, including a high price point, a difficult-to-program architecture, and limited software support. It struggled to compete with the Sega Genesis, Super Nintendo Entertainment System, and later, the Sony PlayStation and Sega Saturn. Despite its commercial failures, the Jaguar has a dedicated fanbase that appreciates its unique hardware and library of games, which includes titles like Alien vs Predator and Tempest 2000. The Jaguar CD, an add-on that allowed for CD-ROM based games, was also released. The console and add-ons had relatively low sales compared to its competition.

platforms.name: Acorn Archimedes
platforms.description: The Acorn Archimedes was a British home computer released in 1987 by Acorn Computers. It was notable for being one of the first widely available home computers to utilize the ARM (Acorn RISC Machine) processor, a Reduced Instruction Set Computing (RISC) architecture that would later become ubiquitous in mobile devices. The Archimedes offered impressive performance for its time, particularly in graphics and multimedia. Its operating system, RISC OS, was designed specifically for the ARM processor and provided a fast and responsive user interface. It supported a range of peripherals and software, and it was a popular choice for educational institutions and enthusiasts in the UK. While it did not achieve widespread commercial success outside of the UK, its technological advancements and the ARM processor's legacy have had a profound impact on the computing industry.
